column5: The best-known clootie well in Britain: a spring by the A832 where the surrounding trees are hung with thousands of rags, left so that illness fades as the cloth rots. Forestry and Land Scotland manages the site and asks for biodegradable cloth only

A walled spring in Culloden Woods, also called Tobar na Coille, where visitors walk sunwise round the well, drink, and tie a rag on a nearby tree. Thousands made the pilgrimage on the first Sunday in May in the 1930s
A rag well recorded in 1885 as visited on the first Sunday of summer. Fresh and fading cloots were still tied at the well during a 2014 visit
A holy well where ribbons were reported tied to the surrounding bushes in 1892. Ribbons and other offerings are still left around it
A lone pine on the fairy hill where the Rev. Robert Kirk is said to have been taken by fairies in 1692. Visitors tie ribbons and cloth to it and the surrounding trees as wishes or fairy offerings
The classic Cornish rag well, described in 1894 as the only Cornish well where rags were traditionally tied. A cloutie tree beside the path is still hung with strips of cloth for healing
A sunken holy well below a cloutie tree that 'guards the entrance' and is hung with rags. Rags have appeared here in roughly the last few decades
A small holy well on private land near St Buryan whose surrounding thorns now carry clouties. The custom here is recent, dating from the last few decades
A holy well near the Iron Age village of Carn Euny with a cloutie tree beside it. The well was said to cure when visited on the first three Wednesdays of May
A small, secluded well on the coast path above St Ives Bay, listed among Cornwall's active cloutie wells
A roadside well whose surrounding trees are 'festooned' with clouties
A village holy well with a few clouties hung beside it
A wooded gorge ending in a waterfall through a rock arch, where rag clouties, ribbons, stacked stones and photos of loved ones are left on every ledge and branch
A 15th-century well-house once used to cure madness by immersion. It has recently become a small rag well with ribbons and other offerings
A medieval well-house that has lately become a rag or clootie well as the custom spreads across Cornwall
The chalk spring that feeds the River Kennet, below West Kennet Long Barrow. The willow over it has become a cloutie tree hung with ribbons and offerings
A Neolithic and Bronze Age stone complex where visitors leave extensive clooties on the trees around the stones. The Pagan Federation has written about the build-up there
The spring where the boy-king Kenelm's body was said to be found. The trees round the replacement wellhead are festooned with rags, ribbons, neckties and tokens
A roofed spring in woodland where rags and coloured strings are still tied to the surrounding trees
A moorland-edge well carved 'Nattie Fonten' where ribbons, cloth strips and dream catchers now hang on the trees and fence. Locals say the rags are a recent addition, not an old custom there
A spring in a cave-like chamber, described as the only currently active rag well in Lincolnshire, with ribbons seen in recent footage
A series of spring pools where St Teilo's skull was once used as a drinking cup for cures. Red and white rags hang on the trees, and it may be the only traditional surviving rag well in Wales
A stone-walled chalybeate well near Harold's Stones. The tree above it is covered with a diverse array of fabric offerings, which are periodically cleared
A holy well beside a ruined post-medieval chapel in woods above Caswell Bay, where rags and objects are currently tied to the trees
Pilgrims dip cloth in the well, rub it on the ailing part, and tie it to the overhanging hawthorns between May Eve and 29 June. Amber pebbles from the well are kept as charms
A large, very cold spring visited at Lughnasa. Clooties, photos, medals and rosaries are tied to a pair of ash trees beside the well
A holy well above Killeavy Old Churches on the pilgrim path up Slieve Gullion, with a rag tree beside it
Three holy wells by a 7th-century church site. A 'Rag Tree' nearby takes a strip of cloth for each petition or thanksgiving
Visitors dip rags in the bullaun water, rub them on warts and hang them on the tree. The tree was mysteriously stripped bare around Christmas 2016
A spring below the ruined church believed to cure eyes. Cloths dipped in it are applied with a prayer and hung on the trees, where hundreds were recorded
